lessons.title: Meaning of Unsupervised Learning
lessons.summary: What it means to learn from unlabeled data: the definition and central idea, what “unlabeled” really means, the general workflow, a visual clustering example, the four kinds of structure (groups, associations, components, anomalies), everyday examples and analogy, unsupervised vs supervised, and its uses and limitations.

content.text: Most machine learning you meet first is supervised: the data comes with the right answers, and the model learns to reproduce them. Unsupervised learning drops the answers entirely. You hand the algorithm a pile of observations with no labels and ask a different question — not “what is the answer?” but “what structure is hiding in here?”

A machine-learning approach where the input data has no known target labels, and the model finds patterns, groups, relationships, or unusual cases on its own by studying similarities, differences, distances, and frequencies.
The model is never told “this is Group A” or “this is Group B.” It decides which observations look similar based only on their features.
content.title: Central idea

content.text: A label is the known answer a supervised model tries to predict. In unsupervised learning, that answer column is simply missing — you have the features but not the outcome.

rows: Not provided — the algorithm must discover possible groups.

content.caption: Figure 1. Before analysis: each point is an observation described by two features, but no group names are supplied.

content.text: “Unlabeled” does not mean the data has no information. It means the data has features, but not the correct output the model should copy.
content.title: Important

content.text: The exact method depends on the algorithm, but the underlying reasoning is usually the same:

items: Collect observations without known target labels.
Describe each observation using measurable features.
Calculate similarity, distance, density, frequency, or another structural signal.
Group observations, discover relationships, reduce complexity, or spot unusual cases.
Interpret the result and decide whether it's useful for the real problem.

content.caption: Figure 2. The general workflow: collect unlabeled data → represent with features → measure similarity → discover hidden structure → interpret the patterns.

content.text: Suppose each point is a customer, positioned by two features — say purchase frequency and average spending. No customer category is given. A clustering algorithm can still find natural groups by looking at which points sit close together.

content.caption: Figure 3. After pattern discovery, similar observations form three groups; the X marks show approximate group centres.

content.text: The colours are added after the algorithm discovers the groups — they are not original answer labels. A human still has to examine each group and decide what it means.
content.title: Interpretation

rows: There's no known output column to predict.
Commonly used to understand an unfamiliar dataset.
Searches for natural groups, relationships, compact representations, or unusual cases.
Many methods use distance, density, correlation, or probability to compare observations.
The machine finds structure; people assign practical meaning.
Different algorithms or settings can produce different but reasonable structures.

content.text: Why can results differ? One person may group objects by colour, another by shape. Likewise, different features, distance measures, and settings can produce different patterns.
content.title: Insight

content.text: A shop has records with age, total spending, visit frequency, and preferred products — but no known customer types. An unsupervised algorithm groups customers with similar behaviour, and the business can later describe the groups as frequent shoppers, occasional shoppers, or high-value customers.

A supermarket can study thousands of baskets and find products that frequently appear together. It's never told which combination is “good” — it discovers repeated associations straight from the purchase records.

content.caption: Figure 4. Illustrative basket frequencies (example values only): Bread + Milk appear together most, then Tea + Biscuits, Rice + Lentils, and so on.

content.text: A bank or security system can learn the normal pattern of transactions or network activity, then flag anything that looks very different as an anomaly. It doesn't prove fraud — it surfaces an unusual case for a human to check.

A dataset may have hundreds of related features. Dimensionality-reduction methods create a smaller set of informative components, making visualisation, storage, and later modelling easier while trying to preserve the important structure.

Imagine opening a drawer full of mixed objects with no name tags. You might place similar colours together, similar shapes together, or similar sizes together. Nobody gives you the correct groups — you create them by noticing patterns. Unsupervised learning follows the same idea, but with mathematical measurements.

content.caption: Figure 5. Sorting mixed items by similarity into groups — an everyday analogy for unsupervised pattern discovery.

rows: Similar customers, documents, images, or patients placed into groups.
Items or events that commonly occur together.
Many features represented with fewer informative components.
Observations that strongly differ from normal patterns.

content.text: The clearest way to grasp “unsupervised” is to line it up against supervised learning.

rows: Predict whether an email is spam
Discover groups of emails with similar content
Use internal measures, stability, or later validation

content.text: Supervised learning learns from answers. Unsupervised learning searches for structure without answer labels.
content.title: Memory rule

items: Most real-world data has no labels, so unsupervised methods can use data that would otherwise be hard to work with.
It reveals patterns people may not notice manually.
It supports data exploration before a supervised model is built.
It can flag segments, trends, or unusual observations for further investigation.
A discovered group is not automatically meaningful or correct in the real world.
The result depends strongly on the chosen features, data quality, algorithm, and settings.
Evaluation is harder because correct labels are usually unavailable.
Human interpretation and domain knowledge are needed before decisions are made.

content.text: Unsupervised learning is not a machine that produces unquestionable truth. It produces mathematical patterns that must be checked for usefulness, stability, bias, and practical meaning.
content.title: Caution

rows: One row or one item in the dataset.
A measurable property describing an observation.
The known answer — not provided in unsupervised learning.
How alike two observations are by their feature values.
A numerical measure of difference between observations.
A group of observations more similar to each other than to others.
A relationship where items or events frequently occur together.
An observation that is unusually different from the common pattern.
A new compressed feature created from several original features.
Features are present, but correct target labels are absent.
To explore data and discover hidden structure.
Groups, associations, compact representations, or anomalies.
Choose suitable features, check results, assign practical meaning.
No labels are supplied; patterns are discovered.

content.text: Unsupervised learning lets a computer examine unlabeled data and discover useful structure. It's mainly exploratory: the machine finds patterns, and people decide what those patterns mean.
content.title: Final takeaway

items: Why is unsupervised learning called “unsupervised”?
What is missing from an unlabeled dataset?
How is a discovered cluster different from a known class label?
Give one example of association discovery.
Why must humans interpret unsupervised-learning results?

keyPoints: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no target labels — features are present, answers are not.
It discovers four main kinds of structure: groups (clustering), relationships (association), compact representations (dimensionality reduction), and unusual cases (anomaly detection).
It is exploratory and similarity-driven: the machine finds mathematical patterns, and people assign practical meaning.
Unlike supervised learning, there is no single guaranteed answer — different features and settings can yield different reasonable structures.
Results must be checked for usefulness, stability, bias, and real-world meaning before any decision.
commonMistakes: Thinking “unlabeled” means the data has no useful information.
Treating a discovered cluster as an automatically correct or meaningful category.
Assuming there is one true answer instead of comparing algorithms and settings.
Acting on results without human interpretation and domain knowledge.

lessons.title: Labelled vs Unlabelled Data
lessons.summary: The distinction that separates supervised from unsupervised learning: what a label is, the definitions of labelled (X, y) and unlabelled (X only) data, a detailed comparison, how removing a target column changes a dataset, the forms a label can take, how each type is used, worked scenarios, a clustering example, and how to identify each type.

content.text: Labels: the one thing that changes everything

Whether a dataset is labelled or not decides which kind of machine learning you can even do with it. It's the single distinction that separates supervised learning from unsupervised learning — so it's worth getting crystal clear on what a “label” actually is.
In machine learning, data is a collection of observations (records). Each record has one or more features — age, temperature, colour, income, attendance, sensor readings, and so on.
The correct target answer attached to a record. It tells a supervised model what output to learn to predict — a category like “spam,” or a number like a house price.
Features describe an observation. A label is the answer or outcome associated with that observation. Column headings are not automatically labels.
content.title: Important distinction

content.caption: Labelled data attaches a correct answer to every record; unlabelled data has the same features but no supplied answer.

content.text: Input features together with a known target value for every training example — supplied by a human, an existing system, an experiment, or a trusted measurement process.

items: Image pixels + “cat” or “dog” class.
Email text + “spam” or “not spam.”
House characteristics + the actual selling price.

content.text: Input features with no correct target answer. The model must examine similarities, differences, density, structure, or unusual behaviour without being told the desired class or number.

items: Customer purchase records with no customer segment.
News articles with no topic category.
Machine sensor readings with no fault label.

content.text: Unsupervised learning is mainly designed for unlabelled data. Its purpose is to discover hidden structure rather than learn from supplied answers.
content.title: Connection to unsupervised learning

rows: X only; no known y in training.
Predict a known category or number.
Often high — labels must be created/verified.
Usually lower at collection — no annotation.
Harder — a single correct answer may not exist.
Wrong or biased labels mislead the model.
Discovered patterns may be hard to interpret or useless.

content.text: The same raw records can be labelled or unlabelled depending on whether a trustworthy target column is available. The distinction is about the presence of a target, not the file format.
content.title: Remember

content.text: The clearest way to see the difference is to look at an actual table. The final column here is the target label.

content.caption: A labelled dataset: the highlighted final column (Segment label) is the target. Remove it and the same records become unlabelled.

items: Feature matrix X: customer age, monthly spending, number of visits.
Target vector y: customer segment, such as Budget, Regular, or Premium.

content.text: If the “Segment label” column is missing, the same records become unlabelled. A clustering algorithm may then group similar customers, but it's not told the names, number, or business meaning of the groups in advance.

content.expression:
Labelled:  Training set = (X, y)
Unlabelled:  Training set = X only
content.explanation: The presence or absence of y is the whole distinction.

content.text: A label can take different forms

rows: Yes / No, Fraud / Genuine, Pass / Fail
Cat / Dog / Bird, Low / Medium / High

content.text: A cluster number from an algorithm is not the same as a true class label. “Cluster 2” has no meaning until a person examines its members and interprets the group.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: How machine learning uses each type
Labelled data teaches a known target; unlabelled data supports pattern discovery.

content.caption: With labelled data, features + known labels train a supervised model to predict labels for new records. With unlabelled data, features alone feed an unsupervised model that discovers groups, structure, or patterns.

items: The model sees both the inputs and the correct answers during training.
It adjusts its parameters to reduce the gap between predictions and known labels.
After training, it predicts labels for new, unseen observations.
The model receives only features — there's no answer key.
It may compute similarity, distance, density, correlation, or lower-dimensional structure.
The output may be clusters, components, associations, or unusual points.

content.text: A mini example makes it concrete. Suppose every fruit record has weight, colour intensity, and diameter:

items: Labelled version: each row also states Apple, Orange, or Banana — a supervised model learns the known categories.
Unlabelled version: the fruit names are missing — an unsupervised model may group fruits with similar measurements.

rows: Each email is marked spam/not spam; a classifier predicts the mark.
No topic labels; a clustering model groups similar messages.
Measurements paired with a confirmed diagnosis.
Measurements but no diagnosis; groups may reveal similar profiles.
Attendance and marks paired with at-risk / not-at-risk.
Records grouped by similar behaviour, no predefined risk classes.
History paired with whether the customer left.
Purchase behaviour used to discover natural groups.

content.caption: Left: every point is the same colour because no class label is supplied. Right: a clustering algorithm separated the points into three similarity-based groups.

items: Left: every point is one colour — no class label is supplied.
Right: a clustering algorithm has separated the points into three similarity-based groups.
The algorithm discovered structure, but a human must still decide what the groups represent.

content.text: In customer data, the three groups might later be read as low-spending occasional customers, regular customers, and high-spending loyal customers. Those names are interpretations, not labels supplied during training.
content.title: Example interpretation

items: It's often easier and cheaper to collect in large quantities.
It can reveal patterns that weren't defined before analysis.
It's useful when experts don't yet know the correct categories.
There may be several reasonable ways to group the same data.
Discovered patterns can reflect noise, scale differences, or irrelevant features.
A cluster's usefulness may need expert judgement or downstream testing.

content.text: Unlabelled data is not necessarily incomplete data. It may be complete for its features while intentionally lacking a target answer.
content.title: Common misconception

rows: Is there a target column (the answer to predict)?
Yes → likely labelled; No → likely unlabelled.
Are target values known for training records?
Does the task predict a predefined outcome?
Does the task find groups or hidden structure?
Is a column merely an identifier (e.g. Student ID)?
An identifier is not a label unless it is the target.

items: Labelled data: most or all records have a target answer.
Unlabelled data: records have features but no target answer.
Partially labelled data: only some records have labels — used in semi-supervised learning.

content.text: Labelled data provides the answer a model should learn; unlabelled data provides only observations from which an unsupervised model must discover useful patterns.
content.title: One-sentence takeaway

items: A dataset has customer spending and age, but no customer segment. Labelled or unlabelled? → Unlabelled.
A dataset has X-ray images and a confirmed disease diagnosis. Labelled or unlabelled? → Labelled.
Why is evaluating unlabelled-data results often harder? → Because there may be no single known correct grouping or pattern to compare against.

keyPoints: A label is the known target answer attached to a record; features describe the record, the label is the outcome.
Labelled data is (X, y) and drives supervised learning; unlabelled data is X only and drives unsupervised learning.
The same records can be labelled or unlabelled depending on whether a trustworthy target column exists — not the file format.
A cluster number is not a true class label; it has no meaning until a human interprets the group.
Unlabelled data is cheaper to collect and reveals undefined patterns, but is harder to evaluate and may reflect noise.
commonMistakes: Treating every column heading (or an identifier like Student ID) as a label.
Assuming unlabelled data is incomplete rather than intentionally lacking a target.
Treating an algorithm's cluster number as a supplied class label.
Expecting a single correct answer when evaluating unlabelled results.

lessons.title: Clustering
lessons.summary: The core unsupervised task of grouping unlabelled data by similarity: cohesion and separation, distance measures, the end-to-end workflow, K-means (steps, inertia, strengths), choosing k with the elbow method and silhouette score, hierarchical clustering and dendrograms, DBSCAN and density, other methods (GMM, K-medoids), evaluation, scaling, a customer-segmentation example, and an algorithm-selection guide.

content.text: Clustering is the workhorse of unsupervised learning. You hand it unlabelled data and it automatically splits the observations into groups — clusters — where points inside a group are more similar to each other than to points in any other group. Nobody tells the algorithm what the groups are; it finds them from the data itself.
An unsupervised technique that divides unlabelled data into groups (clusters) so that points in the same cluster are more similar to one another than to points in other clusters.
High similarity within a cluster and low similarity between different clusters — that's the whole goal.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: In supervised learning, each training example has a known target label. In clustering, the algorithm receives only features and must discover patterns without ever being told the correct group for any observation.
Clustering discovers structure in data — it does not receive the correct group names during training.
content.title: Remember

content.caption: Figure 1. At first the algorithm sees only unlabelled points — the natural groups are hidden.
Figure 2. A clustering algorithm groups similar points and can mark a representative centre (X) for each group.

items: Customer segmentation — group customers by spending, frequency, and preferences.
Document grouping — organise news articles or research papers by topic.
Image segmentation — group similar pixels or image regions.
Anomaly support — small or isolated groups can indicate unusual behaviour.
Biology and medicine — discover patient subgroups or gene-expression patterns.
Social-network analysis — identify communities of strongly connected users.

rows: One item represented by its features.
The mean position of a cluster's points.
An actual data point chosen as the centre.
How tightly points group inside a cluster.
How far different clusters are apart.
A point that fits no meaningful cluster.

content.caption: Figure 3. A useful clustering result has compact groups (high cohesion) with clear gaps between them (high separation).

content.text: Most clustering algorithms rely on a distance or similarity measure. The right one depends on the feature types and what “close” means in your problem.
Distance measures decide what the algorithm considers “similar.” Changing the measure can change the clusters.
content.title: Exam highlight

content.caption: Figure 4. A practical end-to-end clustering workflow — preprocessing, tuning and interpretation all strongly affect the result.

items: Define the purpose — why are groups needed and how will they be used?
Select features — include meaningful similarity variables; remove identifiers and leakage.
Prepare data — handle missing values, outliers, duplicates, and inconsistencies.
Scale features — standardise/normalise numeric variables for distance-based algorithms.
Choose an algorithm — match it to cluster shape, size, noise, and interpretability needs.
Tune parameters — e.g. k in K-means, linkage in hierarchical, eps/min_samples in DBSCAN.
Evaluate — use internal metrics, visualisation, stability, and domain usefulness.
Interpret and name — describe cluster profiles from their feature averages or distributions.

content.text: A centroid-based algorithm that divides numeric data into a chosen number of clusters k, repeatedly assigning each point to its nearest centroid and moving each centroid to the mean of its assigned points.

content.caption: Figure 5. K-means assigns each observation to the nearest centroid, then recomputes the centroids.

items: Choose the number of clusters k.
Initialise k centroids, preferably with k-means++.
Assign every point to the nearest centroid.
Recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points.
Repeat assignment and update until assignments stop changing (or barely improve).

content.text: K-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances (WCSS), also called inertia:

content.expression: J = Σ over clusters [ Σ over points in cluster ‖x − centroid‖² ]
content.explanation: Lower inertia means points sit closer to their centroids. But inertia always drops as k rises, so it can't pick k on its own.

content.text: With k = 3, K-means might discover three behavioural segments — occasional-low-value, frequent-high-value, and frequent-low-value customers. The business names come afterward, by reading the feature profiles.

rows: Simple, fast, scalable to large numeric data.
k must be chosen in advance.
Works best with roughly spherical, similar-sized clusters.
Sensitive to outliers and feature scaling.
Different initial centroids give different local solutions.
Not directly suitable for raw categorical variables.

content.text: Use K-means when features are numeric and scaled, clusters are compact, k is meaningful, and speed matters.
content.title: When to use

content.text: Run K-means for several values of k and plot inertia. Pick the point where adding more clusters gives only a small extra reduction — the bend that looks like an elbow.

content.caption: Figure 6. The elbow (near k = 4 here) balances compactness against model complexity.

content.text: Some datasets show no clear elbow. The method is a heuristic, not a guaranteed answer.
content.title: Limitation

content.text: For each point, the silhouette coefficient compares cohesion within its cluster against separation from the nearest alternative cluster.

content.expression: s = (b − a) / max(a, b)
content.explanation: a = average distance to its own cluster; b = lowest average distance to another cluster.

rows: Average distance to other points in its own cluster.
Lowest average distance to points in another cluster.
Well matched to its cluster, far from alternatives.
May have been assigned to the wrong cluster.

content.caption: Figure 7. A higher average silhouette score generally means better-defined clusters (here k = 4 scores highest).

content.text: The statistically strongest k isn't always the most useful. A retailer may prefer four actionable segments even if five clusters score a slightly higher silhouette. Combine metrics, visualisation, stability, and business or scientific usefulness.
Builds a nested tree of groups without needing a fixed k up front. The final number of clusters is chosen by cutting the tree at a selected height.

rows: Start with every point as its own cluster, then repeatedly merge the closest groups.
Start with all points in one cluster, then repeatedly split groups.
Can chain; sensitive to bridging points.
Compact clusters; common with Euclidean distance.

content.caption: Figure 8. A dendrogram records the order and distance at which groups merge; a horizontal cut sets the number of clusters.

items: Each leaf at the bottom is a data point or small group.
Branches join when clusters merge.
Vertical height shows the distance/dissimilarity at the merge.
A horizontal cut across the tree fixes the number of final clusters.
Large vertical gaps can indicate natural separation.

rows: Can be expensive on large datasets.
No need to commit to k before building.
Results shift with scaling and linkage.
Dendrograms get crowded with many points.

content.text: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise — forms clusters from dense regions and labels isolated observations as noise. It detects irregular shapes and needs no k in advance.

rows: Radius of the neighbourhood around a point.
Too small → much noise; too large → clusters merge.
Minimum neighbours to form a dense region.
Higher demands denser clusters, flags more noise.
Has ≥ min_samples observations within its eps neighbourhood.
Near a core point but lacks enough neighbours itself.
Not density-reachable from any core point; label usually −1.

content.caption: Figure 9. DBSCAN finds the two curved (non-spherical) clusters and explicitly marks scattered points as noise.

rows: Choosing eps and min_samples can be hard.
No need to set the number of clusters.
Distance loses meaning in high dimensions.

content.text: Use DBSCAN when cluster shapes are irregular, noise matters, and density is reasonably consistent.
content.title: When to use

rows: Outliers distort means; real centres preferred.
Soft membership and elliptical clusters needed.
Cluster count should emerge from density.
Each point belongs to exactly one cluster.
K-means assigns A only to Cluster 2.
GMM assigns 70% to Cluster 2, 30% to Cluster 3.

content.text: K-means, hierarchical clustering, and DBSCAN are normally hard-clustering methods; GMM provides soft probabilistic membership.
content.title: Concept check

content.text: Because true labels are usually absent, clustering leans on internal evaluation. No single metric captures usefulness, so combine several checks.

rows: Lower for a fixed k; not comparable everywhere.
Similarity of each cluster to its closest alternative.

content.text: Sometimes reference labels exist only for evaluation, not training. Measures like Adjusted Rand Index, Normalised Mutual Information, and homogeneity compare discovered clusters with known groups — though clustering may reveal valid structures that differ from existing labels.

items: Use scatter plots for two features, or after reducing dimensions with PCA, t-SNE, or UMAP.
Inspect cluster sizes — a tiny cluster may be meaningful, noise, or an artefact.
Compare feature distributions and centroid profiles across clusters.
Check whether clusters overlap strongly or are driven by one dominant feature.
Repeat with different random seeds and samples to test stability.

content.text: Distance-based algorithms can be dominated by features with large numeric ranges. Annual spending in dollars can swamp age in years even when age matters just as much.

content.caption: Figure 10. Without scaling, the spending axis contributes far more to Euclidean distance than the age axis — so scaling matters.

rows: K-means, hierarchical, DBSCAN with bell-shaped features.
Map values to a fixed range (0–1).
When bounded ranges help and outliers are controlled.

items: Handle missing values before computing distances.
Remove duplicate observations if duplicates don't represent real frequency.
Treat extreme outliers, or use robust methods like K-medoids or DBSCAN.
Encode categorical features carefully — one-hot encoding changes distance geometry.
Remove identifiers such as customer ID — they don't represent similarity.
Reduce highly correlated or irrelevant features to avoid noisy dimensions.
Consider PCA for visualisation and for reducing high-dimensional numeric data.

content.text: Clusters can reflect preprocessing choices more than real structure. Always document scaling, encoding, feature selection, and parameter settings.
content.title: Warning

content.text: A retailer wants to group customers using purchase frequency and average order value. No segment labels exist, so clustering is appropriate.

content.caption: Figure 11. K-means reveals three behavioural customer groups in the two-feature space.

content.text: The algorithm outputs cluster IDs like 0, 1, 2. Human analysts study the profiles and assign meaningful names afterward.
content.title: Key lesson

content.text: This scales features, fits three clusters, and computes the average silhouette score. In a real project, test several k values and inspect profiles before deciding.

content.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
model = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
score = silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels)

content.text: The same comparison across four algorithms, split into two tables so it reads on a phone.

rows: No for tree; choose cut later

items: K-means — large, scaled numeric datasets with compact clusters.
Hierarchical — when the nested structure or dendrogram matters.
DBSCAN — when noise and irregular shapes are central.
GMM — when overlapping clusters and membership probabilities are valuable.
K-medoids — when robustness to outliers and real representative centres are needed.

rows: Algorithms impose structure on random data.
A metric can favour a neat but unusable answer.
Treat cluster IDs as arbitrary labels.
Outliers pull centroids and create false groups.
Treat outliers or use robust/density methods.

content.text: Clustering always returns some grouping when forced to. That does not prove natural clusters truly exist.
content.title: Critical warning

items: Clustering is unsupervised because training labels are not provided.
A good cluster has high internal cohesion and strong separation from others.
K-means alternates nearest-centroid assignment with centroid updating.
K-means minimises within-cluster squared distance and needs k in advance.
The elbow method looks for diminishing improvement in inertia.
Silhouette scores near +1 are desirable; negatives suggest poor assignment.
Hierarchical clustering produces a dendrogram and depends on linkage choice.
DBSCAN uses eps and min_samples, finds arbitrary shapes, and identifies noise.
Feature scaling is essential for most distance-based methods.
Evaluation should combine metrics, visualisation, stability, and domain interpretation.

content.text: Clustering finds useful groups in unlabelled data by maximising similarity within groups and separation between groups.
content.title: One-line summary

rows: How is clustering different from classification?
It discovers groups without known labels; classification predicts predefined classes.
Euclidean distance can be dominated by larger-range features.
The mean position of all observations in a cluster.
The sequence and distances at which hierarchical clusters merge.
Can the best silhouette alone decide the solution?
No — it must also be stable, interpretable, and useful.

keyPoints: Clustering groups unlabelled data so points are similar within a cluster and different between clusters — high cohesion, high separation.
K-means needs k in advance, minimises within-cluster squared distance, and requires scaled numeric features.
Choose k by combining the elbow method, silhouette score, stability, and domain usefulness — never one metric alone.
Hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram (cut it to set clusters); DBSCAN finds arbitrary shapes and labels noise without needing k.
Feature scaling is essential for distance-based methods, and any grouping must be checked for real-world meaning — an algorithm always returns clusters.
commonMistakes: Skipping feature scaling before distance-based clustering.
Including ID columns or too many irrelevant features.
Choosing k from a single metric, or assuming clusters must exist.
Reading cluster numbers as ranks or naming clusters before inspecting profiles.

lessons.title: Dimensionality Reduction
lessons.summary: Compressing many features into a smaller informative representation: the curse of dimensionality, feature selection vs extraction, PCA (idea, steps, explained variance, scree plots), other linear methods (SVD, ICA), nonlinear methods (t-SNE, UMAP, kernel PCA, autoencoders), a method-comparison and selection guide, correct scaling and leakage-safe preprocessing, evaluation, and applications.

content.text: Real datasets can have hundreds or thousands of features. Not all of them carry new information — many are redundant, noisy, or strongly correlated. Dimensionality reduction squeezes that wide table down to a smaller, more informative representation while trying to keep the structure that matters.
The number of input features used to describe each observation. A dataset with age, income, height, weight, and study hours has five dimensions.
Representing data with fewer features or components while preserving as much useful information, structure, or variation as possible.

content.caption: Figure 1. The core idea: high-dimensional data → a reduction method (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoder) → lower-dimensional data, for simpler learning and easier visualisation.

content.text: Convert many variables into a smaller, more informative representation.
content.title: One-line idea

rows: Humans can view 2D/3D data, not hundreds of features.
Fewer columns cut memory, training, and prediction time.
Weak, duplicated, or noisy directions can be removed.
A simpler representation may generalise better on limited data.
Images, signals, documents stored with fewer values.
Clusters, trends, and outliers can become easier to detect.
Correlated variables replaced by uncorrelated components.

content.text: More features do not automatically mean more information. Some may be redundant, irrelevant, noisy, or strongly correlated.
content.title: Important

content.text: As the number of features grows, the possible data space expands extremely fast. Observations become sparse, distances become less informative, and a model may need far more examples to learn reliable patterns.

content.caption: Figure 2. As dimensions increase, the amount of data needed to fill the space grows sharply — the data becomes sparse.

content.text: Feature selection keeps some original columns and removes the rest. The retained variables keep their original meaning.

items: Filter methods: variance threshold, correlation, mutual information.
Wrapper methods: test different feature subsets using a model.
Embedded methods: selection happens during training — L1 regularisation or tree importance.

content.text: Feature extraction transforms the original columns into a new, smaller set of components that may combine information from many original variables.

items: Linear extraction: PCA, SVD, ICA.
Nonlinear extraction: t-SNE, UMAP, kernel PCA, autoencoders.

content.caption: Figure 3. The main families of dimensionality-reduction methods, linear and nonlinear.

rows: Keep age and income; drop ID
PC1 = weighted mix of many variables
Compression or structure preservation matters more
Information is compressed into fewer components

content.text: A linear, unsupervised method that transforms correlated features into a smaller set of uncorrelated variables called principal components.

content.caption: Figure 4. Principal components form new directions through the data, capturing the largest spread first.

content.text: PC1 captures the greatest possible variance. PC2 captures the greatest remaining variance while being perpendicular to PC1. Later components follow the same rule.
content.title: Key rule

content.text: For a standardised data matrix X, PCA finds directions w that maximise the projected variance:

content.expression: PC score = X w
content.explanation: The directions come from the eigenvectors of the covariance/correlation matrix; their eigenvalues say how much variance each component explains.

lessons.title: Association-Rule Learning
lessons.summary: Discovering if–then patterns in transaction data: rule anatomy (antecedent → consequent), the transaction–item matrix, the three core measures (support, confidence, lift) with formulas and a fully worked market-basket example, the Apriori algorithm and its property, FP-Growth, an Apriori vs FP-Growth comparison, rule filtering and interpretation pitfalls, applications, and best practices.

content.text: Association-rule learning digs through large datasets to find items that keep showing up together, and expresses those patterns as simple “if–then” rules. It's most famous for market-basket analysis — discovering, for example, that shoppers who buy pasta and sauce often grab cheese too.

An unsupervised technique that discovers interesting relationships, co-occurrences, or if–then patterns among items in large datasets, most often applied to transaction data where each record contains a set of items or events.
It finds items that frequently occur together and expresses the relationship as a rule such as {Bread, Milk} → {Butter}.
content.title: Simple definition

content.text: The algorithm is never given a target label to predict. It explores the data and discovers recurring combinations on its own, producing a collection of rules rather than a single predicted class or number.
“When item or event X occurs, which other item or event Y tends to occur with it?”

items: Retail: customers who buy pasta and sauce may also buy cheese.
Healthcare: patients showing symptoms A and B may frequently show symptom C.
Web analytics: visitors who open page X and page Y may next visit page Z.

rows: A set of transactions/records containing multiple items
Discover frequent itemsets and useful relationships
Rules such as X → Y with quality measures
Healthcare, web usage, fraud, recommendations, manufacturing
A single object, event, or attribute.
A group of one or more items.
One record containing a set of items.
An itemset whose support meets the minimum.
An implication X → Y (X, Y don't overlap).

content.caption: Figure 1. The anatomy of a rule: an antecedent (LHS) implies a consequent (RHS) — IF {Bread, Milk} THEN {Butter}.

content.text: Association-rule algorithms commonly use a binary transaction–item matrix: a 1 means the transaction contains the item, a 0 means it doesn't.

content.caption: Figure 2. An example transaction–item matrix, with a 1 wherever a transaction includes an item.

content.text: Association does not prove causation. A rule only shows that items occur together more or less often than expected — it does not prove one item causes the other.
content.title: Important

content.text: A large dataset can generate thousands of rules. Support, confidence, and lift help rank and filter them.

content.expression: Support(X → Y) = (transactions containing both X and Y) ÷ (total transactions)
content.explanation: How frequently the itemset appears in the whole dataset.

content.text: High support means the rule concerns a common pattern. Very low-support rules may be unreliable or commercially unimportant, even if their confidence is high.

content.expression: Confidence(X → Y) = Support(X ∪ Y) ÷ Support(X)
content.explanation: How often Y appears in transactions that already contain X. Confidence 0.75 means 75% of X-transactions also contain Y.

content.expression: Lift(X → Y) = Confidence(X → Y) ÷ Support(Y)
content.explanation: Compares the observed co-occurrence with what independence would predict.

content.caption: Figure 3. Lift < 1 = negative association, lift = 1 = independent, lift > 1 = positive association.

No association: X and Y behave independently.
Negative: X may reduce the occurrence of Y.
Strength of implication; higher = stronger directional rule.

content.text: A classic algorithm for finding frequent itemsets and generating rules, based on the Apriori property: if an itemset is frequent, all its subsets are frequent — so if an itemset is infrequent, every larger set containing it can be discarded.
All subsets of a frequent itemset must be frequent. This property makes pruning possible and shrinks the search space.
content.title: Apriori property

content.caption: Figure 6. The main stages of Apriori: scan → keep frequent items → generate larger candidates → prune → create rules.

Scan the dataset and compute support for every individual item.
Remove items below minimum support; the rest form frequent 1-itemsets (L1).
Join frequent 1-itemsets to form candidate 2-itemsets (C2).
Count candidate support and prune below minimum support to get L2.
Repeat candidate generation and pruning for 3-itemsets, 4-itemsets, and so on.

Keep rules meeting minimum confidence, then inspect lift and other measures.

lessons.title: K-Means Clustering
lessons.summary: The most common clustering algorithm in depth: the inertia (WCSS) objective, the assignment/centroid-update loop, a fully worked K=2 customer example with Euclidean distances and centroid updates, choosing K with the elbow method and silhouette score, feature scaling and k-means++ initialisation, evaluation, applications, advantages/limits, and a scikit-learn example.

content.text: K-means is the most widely used clustering algorithm, and the one people usually meet first. Give it a number of groups, K, and it partitions your unlabelled data into that many non-overlapping clusters — each observation joining the cluster whose centre (centroid) is nearest. It then refines those centres over and over until they settle.

content.caption: A K-means result for K = 3: the algorithm splits the data into three clusters, each summarised by a centroid (X).

content.text: An unsupervised algorithm that divides a dataset into K non-overlapping clusters, placing each observation in the cluster whose centroid (mean point) is nearest, and repeatedly improving the assignments until the centroids stop changing.
Points inside the same cluster should be as similar and close as possible, while points in different clusters should be comparatively far apart.
content.title: Core idea

content.caption: Figure 1. The algorithm receives unlabelled data — no target class is supplied.

items: There's no labelled output variable such as “fraud/not fraud” or “pass/fail.”
The algorithm discovers structure from feature values and distances.
Cluster numbers are generated by the algorithm and must be interpreted by a human.

A group of observations assigned to the same centroid.

A measure of closeness; Euclidean is most common.

content.text: K-means tries to minimise the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), also called inertia:

content.expression: J = Σᵢ₌₁ᵏ Σₓ∈Cᵢ ‖x − μᵢ‖²
content.explanation: Sum the squared distance from every point to its cluster centroid, across all K clusters.

rows: The objective value (total within-cluster squared error).
The set of observations in cluster i.
The centroid (mean vector) of cluster i.
Squared Euclidean distance between a point and its centroid.

content.text: Smaller inertia means points are packed more tightly around their centroids. But inertia always decreases as K increases, so it cannot be used alone to select K.

content.caption: Figure 2. The assignment and centroid-update steps repeat until assignments or centroids stop changing.

For each cluster, compute the mean of its points — that mean is the new centroid.
Repeat assignment and update until changes are negligible or a max iteration is reached.

content.expression: d(x, μ) = √[(x₁ − μ₁)² + (x₂ − μ₂)²]
content.explanation: Each point goes to whichever centroid is closer.

content.explanation: The new centroid is the average position of the cluster's points.

content.text: Distances are recalculated with the updated centroids. Here the assignments stay the same, so the algorithm has converged.

content.explanation: a = average distance to its own cluster; b = average distance to the nearest other cluster.

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# X contains numerical feature columns only
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

    n_clusters=3,
    init="k-means++",
    n_init=10,
    random_state=42
)
labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)

print("Inertia:", model.inertia_)
print("Silhouette:", silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels))
print("Centroids (scaled space):", model.cluster_centers_)

content.text: Most clustering algorithms need you to name the number of groups, K, before they run — but the “right” number is rarely obvious. Pick well and the clusters capture real structure; pick badly and you either blur genuine groups together or shatter them into meaningless fragments.
Deciding how many groups (K) to create so that observations within a cluster are similar and observations in different clusters are meaningfully different.

lessons.title: Elbow Method
lessons.summary: The classic graphical way to choose K for K-means: what WCSS (inertia) measures and why it always falls as K rises, how to read the bend in the WCSS curve, a worked customer-segmentation example landing on K=3, how different K values divide the same data, a step-by-step procedure with pseudocode, advantages, limitations, common mistakes, and a mini practice.

content.text: K-means can't decide how many clusters to make — you have to tell it K before it runs. The Elbow Method is the classic way to estimate a sensible K: fit the model for a range of K values, measure how tightly each solution groups the data, and look for the point where adding more clusters stops helping much.
A graphical technique for estimating a suitable number of clusters (K) for K-means, by comparing K values using the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS), also called inertia.
Choose the K where adding another cluster stops producing a large improvement. On the graph, that point looks like the bend of a human elbow.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: If K is too small, different natural groups get forced together. If K is too large, meaningful groups get split into unnecessary subgroups.

content.caption: Figure 1. The main steps: choose a range of K → run K-means for each → record WCSS → plot K vs WCSS → select the visible bend.

content.text: WCSS measures how tightly observations cluster around their centroids — it adds up the squared distance between every point and the centroid of the cluster it belongs to.

content.expression: WCSS = Σ (squared distance from each point to its assigned cluster centroid)
content.explanation: Lower means tighter, more compact clusters.

items: Low WCSS: points are close to their centroids, so clusters are compact.
High WCSS: points are far from their centroids, so clusters are spread out.
Important: WCSS always decreases (or stays equal) as K increases, because more centroids fit the data more closely.

content.caption: Figure 2. WCSS is built from the point-to-centroid distances within each cluster.

content.text: The smallest WCSS is not automatically the best choice. If every observation becomes its own cluster, WCSS can reach zero — but that solution is useless.
content.title: Key caution

content.text: A retailer groups customers using two features — annual spending and number of purchases — and tests K-means for K = 1 to 8. The resulting WCSS values, with how much each step improves:
WCSS falls sharply from K = 1 to K = 3, then the reductions become small. So K = 3 is the most reasonable elbow choice.

content.caption: Figure 3. The bend at K = 3 marks diminishing improvement after three clusters.

content.text: The Elbow Method doesn't search for the lowest possible WCSS — it searches for the point where further reduction is no longer worth the extra complexity.

content.text: What the selected K looks like
The same dataset can be divided differently depending on K. The elbow choice is a balance between simplicity and compactness.

content.caption: Figure 4. K = 2 merges natural groups, K = 3 gives a balanced solution, and K = 4 splits one group further.

Draw the curve — K on the horizontal axis, WCSS on the vertical.

lessons.title: Silhouette Score
lessons.summary: The cluster-validation metric that combines cohesion and separation: a(i), b(i) and the s(i) = (b−a)/max(a,b) formula, an interpretation table across the −1 to +1 range, a worked example (0.75), how to read a silhouette plot, using average scores to pick K, silhouette vs elbow, advantages/limitations, best practices, and a scikit-learn example.

content.text: Once a clustering algorithm has grouped your data, how do you know the grouping is any good? The silhouette score answers exactly that. For every point it asks: are you closer to your own cluster than to the nearest neighbouring one? Do that for all points, average it, and you get a single number that rates the whole clustering.
A cluster-validation measure showing how well each data point fits inside its assigned cluster compared with the nearest alternative cluster. Values range from −1 to +1.

items: It's used after a clustering algorithm has assigned points to clusters.
It works with many distance-based results, such as K-means and hierarchical clustering.
It gives a value for each observation and an average for the whole solution.
The coefficient ranges from −1 to +1.

content.text: A good point should be close to other points in its own cluster and far from points in the nearest neighbouring cluster.
content.title: Core idea

content.caption: Better-separated clusters (left) produce high positive silhouettes; overlapping clusters (right) give near-zero or negative ones.

s(i) = [ b(i) − a(i) ] / max{ a(i), b(i) }
Overall score = average of s(i) over all observations
content.explanation: Tight cohesion (small a) and strong separation (large b) push s toward +1.

content.text: The score is not defined for a solution with only one cluster, and each cluster should contain enough observations for a meaningful comparison.

Insert a(i) and b(i) into the formula to get s(i).
Repeat for all observations.
Average all s(i) values to obtain the overall silhouette score.

    labels = model.fit_predict(X)
    score = silhouette_score(X, labels)

content.text: Instead of forcing your data into a fixed number of groups, hierarchical clustering builds a whole family tree of clusters — showing how individual points join into small groups, how those merge into bigger ones, and so on up to a single cluster containing everything. You then “cut” the tree wherever a sensible number of clusters appears.

An unsupervised technique that groups similar observations into a nested tree of clusters, without predefined labels — showing how small clusters combine into larger ones (or how a large cluster divides into smaller ones).
Objects that are more similar join earlier in the hierarchy; dissimilar objects join later, at a greater distance.

content.text: A dendrogram is the signature picture of hierarchical clustering — a tree that shows, step by step, how individual observations get merged into ever-larger groups. Read it well and you can see which items are most alike, spot natural groupings, and decide how many clusters your data really has.

A tree-shaped diagram showing the sequence in which observations or smaller clusters are merged during hierarchical clustering — from separate observations at the bottom to one complete cluster at the top.
Items that merge at a low height are relatively similar. Items or clusters that merge at a high height are relatively dissimilar.

content.text: A dendrogram usually comes from agglomerative clustering: every observation starts in its own cluster, and at each step the two closest observations or clusters merge, until everything belongs to one cluster.

lessons.title: DBSCAN
lessons.summary: Density-based clustering: core/border/noise points, the eps and MinPts parameters and their interaction, the density-reachable chain that lets clusters follow irregular shapes, the algorithm and a worked example, choosing eps with a k-distance graph and MinPts ≥ D+1, a scikit-learn implementation, evaluation, a comparison with K-means and hierarchical clustering, applications, and common mistakes.

content.text: K-means asks “how many round groups are there?” DBSCAN asks a different question: “where is the data densely packed?” It grows clusters outward through connected dense neighbourhoods, follows whatever shape the data takes, and simply labels the lonely points as noise instead of forcing them into a group.

Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise — an unsupervised method that finds regions of many nearby points, grows clusters where dense neighbourhoods connect, and labels points in sparse regions as noise.

Unlike centroid-based methods, DBSCAN doesn't force every observation into a cluster and doesn't need the number of clusters up front. That makes it ideal when clusters have curved, elongated, ring-shaped, or otherwise irregular boundaries.
DBSCAN groups closely packed points, expands clusters through connected dense neighbourhoods, and treats points in sparse regions as noise.

rows: Yes — noise gets label −1 in scikit-learn
Clusters of similar density in a meaningful distance space

content.text: MinPts is how many points must be in an ε-neighbourhood for the centre to count as a core point. A larger value demands stronger evidence of density and makes the algorithm less sensitive to small accidental groups.

content.caption: Figure 2. Changing ε can fragment clusters (too small), give a balanced solution, or merge different groups (too large).

Find all observations within distance ε of it.
If the neighbourhood has ≥ MinPts observations, mark it a core point and start/expand a cluster.
Inspect each neighbour — when another core point is found, add its neighbours too, forming a chain of density-connected points.
Points reached from a core point but not dense enough themselves become border points.
A point that can't connect to any core region is labelled noise.
Repeat until all observations have been visited.

content.text: The chain concept is why DBSCAN can follow complex shapes. It never requires every point to be near one centre — instead, local dense neighbourhoods connect into a complete cluster.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# X contains only the features used for clustering
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

model = DBSCAN(
    eps=0.35,
    min_samples=5,
    metric="euclidean"
)
labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)

# -1 represents noise; 0, 1, 2, ... represent clusters
n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_noise = np.sum(labels == -1)

print("Clusters:", n_clusters)
print("Noise points:", n_noise)

lessons.title: Gaussian Mixture Models
lessons.summary: Probabilistic soft clustering: data as a weighted mixture of Gaussians, responsibilities and the mixing-weight/mean/covariance parameters, the EM algorithm (E-step and M-step) with its formulas, a worked 1-D example, covariance types (spherical/diagonal/tied/full) and cluster shape, choosing components with AIC/BIC, a comparison with K-means and DBSCAN, a scikit-learn example, applications, and common mistakes.

content.text: What a Gaussian Mixture Model is

K-means gives every point a single hard label. A Gaussian Mixture Model does something richer: it assumes the data was generated by several overlapping bell-shaped (Gaussian) distributions and, for each point, reports the probability that it came from each one. The result is soft clustering — uncertainty is kept, not thrown away.
A probabilistic model assuming the data was generated from a mixture of several Gaussian distributions, where each component represents a hidden subgroup or data-generating pattern.

content.caption: Figure 1. Three weighted Gaussian components sum into one overall mixture density.

items: Mixture: the whole dataset is treated as a combination of several hidden distributions.
Gaussian: each hidden component is a normal distribution with its own centre and spread.
Probabilistic: the output is probabilities, not only hard cluster labels.
Latent variable: the true component that generated a point is hidden and must be inferred.

content.text: Picture customer spending with three overlapping groups — low, regular, and premium spenders. A customer near a boundary might be 55% regular and 45% premium. A GMM represents that uncertainty directly.
Instead of forcing each point into exactly one cluster, a GMM estimates the probability that the point belongs to every component. That's soft clustering.
content.title: Key idea

content.caption: Figure 2. A boundary point receives a probability for each component rather than one forced label.

content.text: The estimated probability r(i,k) that component k generated observation i. For every observation, the responsibilities across all K components sum to 1.

content.expression: r(i,k) = P(zᵢ = k | xᵢ)
content.explanation: The posterior probability that component k is responsible for observation xᵢ.

items: Customer A → mostly Component 1.
Customer B → uncertain: Components 1 and 2 overlap.
Customer C → mostly Component 3.

content.text: For K Gaussian components, the density of an observation x is the weighted sum of the component densities:

content.expression: p(x) = Σₖ πₖ · N(x | μₖ, Σₖ)
content.explanation: The mixing weights satisfy πₖ ≥ 0 and Σ πₖ = 1.

rows: Expected proportion of data from component k.
Spread, scale, direction, and shape of component k.
Unobserved component identity for observation i.

content.explanation: You don't need every symbol — μ controls location, Σ controls shape. The covariance lets components be circles, axis-aligned ellipses, or tilted ellipses.

content.caption: Figure 3. A fitted GMM can represent overlapping clusters with different elliptical shapes.

content.text: The component labels are unknown, so direct estimation is hard. GMMs are fitted with the Expectation-Maximisation (EM) algorithm — an iterative loop that alternates between estimating hidden memberships and updating parameters.

content.caption: Figure 4. EM alternates the E-step (estimate responsibilities) and M-step (update parameters) until the log-likelihood converges.

items: Choose K and initialise means, covariance matrices, and mixing weights.
E-step: calculate the responsibility of every component for every observation.
M-step: update each component using the responsibility-weighted data.
Calculate the log-likelihood of the data under the updated model.
Repeat E-step and M-step until the likelihood barely changes or the iteration limit is reached.

content.expression: r(i,k) = [πₖ N(xᵢ | μₖ, Σₖ)] / [Σⱼ πⱼ N(xᵢ | μⱼ, Σⱼ)]
content.explanation: The numerator is component k's weighted density; the denominator normalises across all components.

content.expression: Nₖ = Σᵢ r(i,k)     μₖ = (1/Nₖ) Σᵢ r(i,k) xᵢ
content.explanation: Nₖ is the effective number of observations assigned to component k.

content.expression: Σₖ = (1/Nₖ) Σᵢ r(i,k)(xᵢ − μₖ)(xᵢ − μₖ)ᵀ     πₖ = Nₖ / n
content.explanation: Covariance and weight are updated from the responsibility-weighted data.

content.text: EM can converge to a local optimum. Different random initialisations may give different solutions, so multiple starts (e.g. n_init > 1) are recommended.
content.title: Important limitation

content.text: Take the values 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10 and fit a two-component GMM. After several EM iterations, the model estimates:

content.explanation: For x = 3, the first Gaussian has much higher density, so it takes nearly all the responsibility.

content.text: For a boundary value such as x = 5.5 the probabilities may be close to 0.50 and 0.50. That's the benefit of soft clustering — uncertainty is preserved instead of hidden.
The covariance structure is one of the most important GMM choices — it sets how flexible the cluster shapes can be and how many parameters must be estimated.

content.caption: Figure 5. Covariance options control the size, orientation, and flexibility of the Gaussian components.

All components share one full covariance.
Same shape and orientation for every component.
Each component its own full covariance.

content.text: Start with full covariance for modest-dimensional data when clusters may be tilted. Try diagonal covariance with many features or limited data, since it estimates fewer parameters.

content.text: GMM needs K. Increasing K almost always improves the training likelihood, but too many components overfit. Information criteria balance fit against complexity.

content.expression: AIC = 2p − 2 log(L)     BIC = p log(n) − 2 log(L)
content.explanation: p = number of estimated parameters, n = observations, L = maximised likelihood. Lower is better.

content.caption: Figure 6. The preferred model is usually near the minimum AIC or BIC value (K = 4 here).

from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

lessons.title: Principal Component Analysis
lessons.summary: The standard linear dimensionality-reduction method: components as variance-maximising orthogonal axes, key terms (eigenvectors, eigenvalues, loadings, scores), the five-step mathematics (standardise → covariance → eigenproblem → explained variance → projection), a worked two-feature example, choosing k with explained variance and a scree plot, interpreting loadings, a leakage-safe workflow with scikit-learn, applications, comparisons, and mistakes.

content.text: When a dataset has dozens or hundreds of numerical features, many of them say the same thing in slightly different ways. Principal Component Analysis finds a smaller set of new axes — principal components — that capture as much of the variation as possible, so you can compress, visualise, and de-noise the data while keeping most of its information.

An unsupervised technique that transforms correlated numerical features into a smaller set of uncorrelated variables (principal components), each a linear combination of the originals, ordered by how much variance they capture.

items: The principal components are linear combinations of the original features.
They are mutually orthogonal (uncorrelated in the transformed space).
The first component captures the greatest possible variance.
Each later component captures the greatest remaining variance while staying perpendicular to earlier ones.

content.text: PCA replaces many possibly correlated numerical features with fewer uncorrelated principal components while retaining as much variation as possible.

content.text: PCA doesn't use a target label. It examines only the structure and variation of the input features — which is why it's unsupervised.

content.text: Picture a cloud of points stretched diagonally. The original horizontal and vertical axes don't describe its main direction well. PCA rotates the coordinate system so the first new axis follows the longest direction of the cloud.

content.text: PCA reduces to five conceptual steps.

content.expression: Step 1 — Centre / standardise:  z = (x − mean) / standard deviation
content.explanation: Centring puts each feature at zero; dividing by the standard deviation gives comparable scale.

content.expression: Step 2 — Covariance matrix:  C = (1 / (n − 1)) Xᵀ X
content.explanation: Summarises how the standardised features vary together.

content.expression: Step 3 — Eigenproblem:  C v = λ v
content.explanation: Each eigenvector v is a component direction; its eigenvalue λ is the variance captured there.

content.expression: Step 4 — Explained variance:  EVRᵢ = λᵢ / Σλ
content.explanation: Rank eigenvalues largest to smallest; ratios show how much variance each component explains.

content.expression: Step 5 — Projection:  T = X Wₖ
content.explanation: Wₖ holds the top k eigenvectors; T is the reduced dataset of component scores.

content.text: Most modern libraries compute PCA efficiently using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), but the interpretation is the same.

content.text: Standardise features when they use different units or have very different ranges — otherwise a large-scale feature can dominate the principal components.

content.text: Eight students are described by two correlated features — weekly study hours and practice questions completed. The raw and standardised values (split into two tables for width):

content.text: PC1 explains about 99.9% of the variance, so the two features can be represented by one component with very little loss. High PC1 scores are students high on both study hours and practice questions.

content.text: If only PC1 is retained, the reduced dataset holds one value per student instead of two.

The number of components k balances simplicity against information retention. There's no universal percentage, but 80%, 90%, 95%, or 99% cumulative explained variance are common thresholds depending on the application.

content.caption: Figure 3. In this scree plot, the first four components retain 93% of total variance (past the 90% target).

rows: Point after which gains are small.

content.text: The elbow method in PCA uses explained variance; the elbow method in K-means usually uses within-cluster sum of squares. The graphs look similar, but the quantities differ.

content.text: A component is interpreted through its loadings. Large positive or negative loadings mean a feature strongly influences that component.

content.caption: Figure 4. Example loadings: PC1 is a general engagement component, PC2 mainly a sleep-quality component.

items: Same signs: features increase together along the component.
Opposite signs: one increases while another decreases along the component.
Large absolute value: strong contribution to the component.

lessons.title: t-SNE Introduction
lessons.summary: A nonlinear visualisation technique for high-dimensional data: preserving local neighbourhoods, the four-step process (high-D similarities → initial map → t-distribution → minimise KL divergence), the parameters (especially perplexity), a worked customer example, how t-SNE compares with PCA, how to read a t-SNE plot without overclaiming, strengths and limitations, a scikit-learn workflow, and a trust checklist.

content.text: Some datasets have hundreds or thousands of features — far too many to see at once. t-SNE takes that high-dimensional data and squeezes it down to a 2-D or 3-D map where similar observations land close together, so you can actually look at the structure. It's built for exploration and visualisation, not prediction.
t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding — an unsupervised, nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique mainly used to visualise high-dimensional data in two or three dimensions.
For example, an image dataset may have hundreds of pixel features per image. t-SNE can compress those into two coordinates so that visually similar images appear as nearby points on a scatter plot.
t-SNE creates a visual map in which observations that are similar in the original high-dimensional dataset are placed close together in a 2-D or 3-D plot.
content.title: Simple definition

content.caption: Figure 1. A t-SNE map showing four visually separated local groups from an 8-dimensional dataset.

content.text: t-SNE is primarily a visualisation and exploratory-analysis method. It is not automatically a clustering algorithm, classifier, or proof that natural classes exist.
content.title: Important

content.text: Humans can directly visualise only one, two, or three dimensions, yet ML datasets often have tens, hundreds, or thousands of features. t-SNE produces a low-dimensional representation that's easier to inspect.

items: Visual exploration: reveals possible clusters, subgroups, and neighbourhood patterns.
Quality checking: helps identify unusual observations or mixed groups.
Feature-learning inspection: shows whether learned embeddings separate meaningful categories.
Communication: turns complex numerical representations into an understandable scatter plot.

content.text: The central purpose of t-SNE is to preserve local similarity. If two observations are close in the original space, t-SNE tries to place them close in the low-dimensional map. Far-away relationships get less emphasis.

content.caption: Figure 2. Nearby observations are encouraged to stay nearby; exact distances between far groups are less reliable.

rows: May suggest a subgroup worth investigating.
No guarantee of true global distance.
Don't treat area as exact density or volume.

content.caption: Figure 3. The simplified t-SNE workflow: prepare data → choose settings → build similarities → optimize layout → interpret carefully.

content.text: Step 1: measure similarity in high dimensions

For each observation, t-SNE calculates how likely other observations are to be its neighbours. Close points get high similarity probabilities, distant points low ones — a Gaussian-style similarity in the original feature space.
Step 2: create an initial low-dimensional map
The algorithm starts with initial 2-D or 3-D coordinates, either random or from a PCA initialisation. This first map usually doesn't preserve the required neighbour relationships yet.
Step 3: compare high- and low-dimensional similarities

In the low-dimensional map, t-SNE uses a heavy-tailed Student t-distribution. This keeps moderately distant points separated and reduces the crowding problem — where too many observations would otherwise be forced into a small central region.
t-SNE repeatedly moves points to reduce the difference between the high- and low-dimensional similarity distributions, measured with Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence.

content.expression: Minimise KL(P || Q)
content.explanation: P = neighbour similarities in the original space; Q = neighbour similarities in the 2-D/3-D map. A lower value means local relationships are represented more consistently.

content.caption: Figure 4. KL divergence falls during optimisation (illustrative; actual curves vary by dataset and settings).

rows: 2 for a scatter plot; 3 for interactive views.
Test e.g. 5, 30, 50; must be below the sample count.
Automatic settings are a practical start.

PCA init is often more stable than random.

content.text: Perplexity is one of the most discussed settings — an approximate balance between paying attention to very close neighbours and considering a wider local region. There's no single best value, so compare several.

rows: Strong focus on tiny local neighbourhoods.
May fragment one structure into many islands.
Balances local detail and wider context.
May smooth or merge small local differences.

content.caption: Figure 5a. The same data at perplexity = 5 — very local focus, groups look fragmented.
Figure 5b. Perplexity = 30 — a balanced layout with four clear groups.
Figure 5c. Perplexity = 80 — tighter, broader neighbourhoods. Rely on patterns stable across settings, not one layout.

content.text: A retail dataset has one row per customer with seven standardised features — annual spending, visit frequency, average basket value, discount usage, online activity, return rate, and loyalty duration. content.text: Both reduce dimensionality, but with different goals: PCA is linear and seeks directions of maximum variance; t-SNE is nonlinear and emphasises local neighbourhood similarity.

content.caption: Figure 6. A PCA projection of the same 8-D data — compare with the t-SNE map (Figure 1). t-SNE often shows local separation more clearly; PCA gives a more globally interpretable linear projection.

content.text: A common introductory workflow: clean the data, encode categoricals, scale the features, optionally reduce very high dimensions with PCA first, run t-SNE, and plot the two output coordinates.

content.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# X contains numerical feature columns only
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

embedding = TSNE(
    n_components=2,
    perplexity=30,
    learning_rate="auto",
    init="pca",
    max_iter=1000,
    random_state=42
).fit_transform(X_scaled)

plt.scatter(embedding[:, 0], embedding[:, 1], s=18)
plt.xlabel("t-SNE dimension 1")
plt.ylabel("t-SNE dimension 2")
plt.title("t-SNE visualization")
plt.show()

lessons.title: Association Rules & Support
lessons.summary: The three evaluation metrics behind association rules: support (how common X and Y are together), confidence (how often Y follows X, and why it's directional), and lift (co-occurrence versus chance). Includes formulas, a shared five-transaction worked example, a full six-rule calculation table, how rules are generated, threshold choices, and how to judge a rule's usefulness.

content.text: Association-rule mining looks through transaction data for items that keep turning up together and writes each pattern as an “if–then” rule. This lesson focuses on the three numbers that decide whether such a rule is worth trusting: support, confidence, and lift.
An unsupervised co-occurrence pattern written as X → Y: when itemset X occurs, itemset Y tends to occur as well. X is the antecedent, Y the consequent.
An association rule shows a relationship, not causation. X → Y does not prove that X causes Y.
content.title: Important

content.caption: Figure 1. The association-rule mining workflow: transaction data → frequent itemsets → candidate rules → measure support/confidence/lift → keep useful rules.

items: Market-basket analysis: products customers commonly buy together.
Website behaviour: pages or actions that often occur in the same session.
Healthcare pattern analysis: symptoms or treatments that co-occur in records.
Recommendation support: suggesting related items based on past combinations.

rows: A group of one or more items.
One record containing a set of items.
The left side of a rule.
The right side of a rule.

content.text: These five transactions are used throughout, so all the calculations can be compared on one dataset.

content.caption: Figure 2. A visual representation of the running transaction dataset.

content.text: How frequently the complete rule itemset appears in the whole dataset. For X → Y, it's the proportion of transactions containing both X and Y.

content.expression: Support(X → Y) = Count(X and Y) / Total transactions
content.explanation: Ranges from 0 to 1; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

content.caption: Figure 3. Support is based on the overlap between transactions containing X and those containing Y.

items: Transactions with both Diaper and Beer: T2, T3, T4 = 3.
Total transactions = 5.

content.text: Diaper and Beer occur together in 60% of all transactions.
content.title: Interpretation

items: It removes rules based on very rare combinations.
It highlights patterns that affect a meaningful portion of the dataset.
A high-confidence rule can still be unreliable when its support is extremely low.

content.text: How often Y occurs among the transactions that already contain X — an estimate of the conditional probability of Y given X.

content.expression: Confidence(X → Y) = Support(X and Y) / Support(X) = Count(X and Y) / Count(X)
content.explanation: Ranges from 0 to 1.

items: Transactions with Diaper: T2, T3, T4, T5 = 4.
Transactions with both Diaper and Beer: T2, T3, T4 = 3.
Confidence = 3 / 4 = 0.75 = 75%.

content.text: Among transactions containing Diaper, 75% also contain Beer.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Confidence is directional — X → Y and Y → X can differ because the denominator changes.
Don't reverse a rule automatically. The same item pair can produce different confidence values in opposite directions — here 75% one way, 100% the other.
content.title: Direction

content.text: Compares the observed confidence of X → Y with the confidence expected if X and Y were independent — correcting for how common Y already is.

content.expression: Lift(X → Y) = Confidence(X → Y) / Support(Y) = Support(X and Y) / [Support(X) × Support(Y)]
content.explanation: Two equivalent forms of the same measure.

items: Confidence(Diaper → Beer) = 0.75.
Support(Beer) = 3 / 5 = 0.60.

content.text: A transaction containing Diaper is 1.25 times as likely to contain Beer as a randomly selected transaction.
content.title: Interpretation

content.caption: Figure 4. Lift interpretation around the independence baseline of 1.

rows: X and Y occur together more often than expected.
Knowing X doesn't change the likelihood of Y.
X and Y occur together less often than expected.

content.text: The three answer different questions, split across two tables for width.

rows: How common is X with Y?
When X occurs, how often does Y?
Can miss rare but valuable patterns.
Can be inflated when Y is already common.
High values may be unstable at very low support.

content.text: Evaluate all three together. Support checks prevalence, confidence checks directional reliability, and lift checks whether the rule beats the baseline frequency of the consequent.
content.title: Best practice

content.caption: Figure 5. Support, confidence and lift for selected rules from the example dataset (lift = 1 baseline dashed).

content.text: Eggs → Beer has high confidence and lift but only 20% support — it's based on one transaction, so treat it cautiously.

content.text: Six rules from the example, split into their metrics and their verdicts.
