Positive but based on only two baskets.

content.text: Association-rule mining follows two linked stages — frequent-itemset discovery, then rule evaluation — usually as these steps:

items: Prepare transactions — represent each record as a set of items (one-hot or transaction format).
Set minimum support — remove itemsets too rare for the objective.
Find frequent itemsets — Apriori or FP-Growth identify combinations meeting minimum support.
Generate directional rules — split each frequent itemset into antecedent and consequent possibilities.
Filter by confidence and lift — keep rules that are reliable and stronger than the baseline.
Check usefulness — consider sample size, redundancy, business value, and whether the rule supports an action.

content.text: There's no universal threshold — suitable values depend on dataset size, item frequency, and the cost of acting on a rule.

rows: May drop rare but meaningful patterns.

content.text: Explore several threshold combinations, then inspect the number and quality of the resulting rules. Don't pick thresholds solely to maximise the rule count.
content.title: Practical starting point

content.text: Judging whether a rule is useful

items: Adequate support: enough transactions to be credible.
Good confidence: Y frequently follows X in the records.
Lift above 1: the rule improves on the general popularity of Y.
Non-redundancy: it adds information beyond a simpler or stronger rule.
Actionability: a decision, recommendation, or investigation can be based on it.
Domain sense: the relationship is plausible, not a recording artefact.

content.text: Beer → Diaper: support 60%, confidence 100%, lift 1.25. It's supported by three of five baskets, always holds in this sample, and beats chance — more defensible than Eggs → Beer, which rests on a single basket.
content.title: Example decision

rows: Check lift — a common consequent inflates confidence.
A rule on one or two records is unstable even at 100% confidence.
Confidence changes with direction (antecedent count changes).
Lift can far exceed 1 when the consequent is rare.
Remove redundant, trivial, and non-actionable rules.

content.text: Support = popularity of the complete rule. Confidence = reliability in one direction. Lift = improvement over chance.
content.title: Memory trick

items: In 200 transactions, 40 contain Tea and Biscuits. Support(Tea → Biscuits)? → 40/200 = 0.20 (20%).
Tea appears in 50 transactions, Tea+Biscuits in 40. Confidence? → 40/50 = 0.80 (80%).
If Support(Biscuits) = 0.50, lift of Tea → Biscuits? → 0.80/0.50 = 1.60.
What does lift below 1 mean? → X and Y co-occur less than expected — a negative association.
Why can a 100%-confidence rule still be weak? → It may rest on very few transactions, or the consequent may already be extremely common — check support and lift.

content.text: A strong association rule is not simply the one with the highest confidence. It should have meaningful support, confidence, lift above 1 (for positive association), and practical usefulness.
content.title: Core conclusion

keyPoints: Support = Count(X and Y) / N — how common the whole rule is; it filters out very rare, unreliable combinations.
Confidence = Count(X and Y) / Count(X) — how often Y follows X; it's directional, so X→Y and Y→X can differ.
Lift = Confidence / Support(Y) — above 1 is a positive association, 1 is independence, below 1 is negative.
Confidence alone misleads when the consequent is common — always read support and lift together.
A strong rule needs meaningful support, good confidence, lift above 1, non-redundancy, and real-world usefulness.
commonMistakes: Reading an association rule as causation.
Judging rules by confidence alone instead of also using lift.
Trusting a 100%-confidence rule that rests on one or two transactions.
Assuming X→Y and Y→X have the same confidence.

lessons.title: Anomaly Detection
lessons.summary: Finding observations that differ from normal behaviour: why it's usually unsupervised, the three anomaly types (point, contextual, collective), the main method families (statistical Z-score/IQR, distance/density k-NN/LOF, clustering, Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, autoencoders) with a comparison, a worked sensor example, turning anomaly scores into alerts via thresholds, evaluation metrics, applications, challenges, and a method-selection guide.

content.text: Fraud, machine faults, and network intrusions all share one trait: they don't look like the everyday, normal data around them. Anomaly detection is the art of learning what “normal” looks like, measuring how far each observation strays from it, and flagging the strangest ones for a human to investigate.
The process of identifying observations, events, or patterns that differ significantly from the behaviour considered normal in a dataset.
In unsupervised learning, the model usually gets data without reliable “normal” or “fraud” labels. It learns the dominant structure of the data and gives unusual observations a high anomaly score.

content.caption: Figure 1. Anomalies (A1–A4) lie far from the dense cloud of normal observations.

content.text: Learn what normal data looks like, measure how different each new observation is, and flag highly unusual ones for investigation.
content.title: Simple idea

Is this point far from normal?

lessons.title: Advantages and Limitations
lessons.summary: Weighs the strengths of unsupervised learning — no labels needed, hidden-pattern discovery, exploration, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction, and feature creation — against its limitations: hard-to-evaluate results, interpretability challenges, sensitivity to scaling and parameters, instability, computational cost, and bias. Includes a balanced comparison, a customer-segmentation case study, and an eight-step workflow for more reliable results.

content.text: Unsupervised learning is powerful precisely because it works without labelled outcomes — but that same freedom is also its biggest weakness. This lesson lays the strengths and the risks side by side so you know when to reach for these methods, when to be cautious, and how to make the results more trustworthy.

content.caption: Core idea: unsupervised methods take unlabelled data and discover useful structure — groups, relationships, outliers, and compact features — without a predefined target label.

content.text: A machine-learning approach that studies data without a predefined target label, aiming to discover hidden structure such as groups, associations, unusual observations, or lower-dimensional representations.
Because there is no known “correct answer” for every record, unsupervised learning is powerful for discovery but harder to evaluate than supervised learning.
content.title: Key idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on the advantages and limitations. Algorithm details appear only where they help explain a benefit or a risk.
content.title: Scope

content.text: The same feature that makes unsupervised learning attractive — working without labelled outcomes — also creates its biggest challenge. It can reveal patterns that were never expected, but those patterns may not always be meaningful, stable, or useful. Every result must therefore be interpreted with domain knowledge and validation checks.

rows: Uses large amounts of naturally available data
No direct ground truth for judging correctness
Can find unexpected groups and relationships
May surface patterns that are statistically present but practically weak
Supports clustering, anomaly detection, and compression
Different algorithms or parameters may give different answers

content.text: Labelling data can require experts, time, and money. Unsupervised methods can begin with raw datasets in which only the input features are available.
Example: a retailer can group thousands of customers by purchasing behaviour even when no customer-segment labels already exist.
The model is not restricted to predicting a known class. It can expose natural groups, correlations, unusual records, or repeated combinations that analysts did not define in advance.
Example: clustering may reveal a small group of high-value customers who buy infrequently but spend heavily.
Unsupervised learning helps analysts understand the shape, structure, and diversity of a dataset before building predictive models or making decisions.
Example: a scatter plot after dimensionality reduction may show that two product categories overlap strongly.
Rare observations can be identified by their distance, density, reconstruction error, or unusual behaviour compared with most of the data.
Example: a manufacturing sensor pattern that differs from normal operating cycles can be flagged for inspection.
Methods such as PCA can summarise many correlated features into fewer components while preserving much of the useful variation.
Example: fifty sensor variables may be compressed into five components for visualisation and faster modelling.
Clusters, embeddings, or components can become new features for later supervised models. In some workflows, discovered groups are used as provisional labels for further review.
Example: a document cluster ID can be added as a feature in a recommendation system.
Automated pattern discovery can process far more records than manual inspection, especially when data arrives continuously.
Example: an e-commerce platform can routinely group products by behaviour instead of manually classifying every item.

content.caption: Figure 1. Illustrative view of major unsupervised-learning strengths (conceptual, not empirical scores).

content.text: There may be no true label or known output against which the discovered result can be compared. Internal metrics such as the silhouette score are useful, but they do not prove that clusters are meaningful for the real problem.
A high-scoring cluster solution may still be useless to a business if the groups do not support decisions.
content.title: Risk

content.text: Results can be difficult to interpret
A model may discover mathematically valid structures that are hard to explain in human terms. Components, embeddings, or clusters do not automatically have clear names or meanings.
Risk example: a cluster defined by a complex combination of twenty features can be very difficult to describe.
Sensitive to feature scaling and data quality
Large-scale variables can dominate distance-based methods. Missing values, outliers, duplicate records, irrelevant features, and measurement errors can all distort the discovered structure.
Risk example: income measured in thousands may dominate age measured in years unless features are scaled.
Algorithm and parameter choices strongly affect results
The number of clusters, distance measure, neighbourhood radius, minimum samples, linkage method, and initialisation can all change the output.
Risk example: choosing k = 2 or k = 5 can divide the same customer data into very different segments.
Discovered patterns may not be stable
Small changes in the sample, random initialisation, or preprocessing may produce different groups. Unstable solutions reduce confidence and practical usefulness.
Risk example: customers may switch clusters after a small data update, making segment-based campaigns inconsistent.
Computational and memory costs can be high
Some algorithms become expensive for large datasets, high dimensions, or pairwise distance calculations. Repeated tuning and stability tests add further cost.
Risk example: hierarchical clustering may be impractical when millions of observations must be compared.
Can reinforce bias or misleading structure
Historical data may contain social, operational, or sampling biases. The model can reproduce these patterns without understanding whether they are fair, ethical, or appropriate.
Clusters based on location and spending may indirectly separate protected or disadvantaged groups.
content.title: Risk

content.text: Not always suitable for direct decision-making
Unsupervised outputs often require expert review before action. A cluster is not automatically a prediction, diagnosis, or causal explanation.
Risk example: an anomaly flag shows that a record is unusual, not that it is definitely fraudulent or faulty.

content.text: Good practice turns limitations into manageable risks. A clear, repeatable workflow makes unsupervised results far more reliable.

content.caption: Figure 4. A practical workflow for improving the reliability of unsupervised-learning results: clarify purpose, prepare data, compare methods, and validate meaning.

items: Define the purpose first — decide whether the goal is segmentation, anomaly screening, association discovery, or dimensionality reduction. A clear purpose guides method and validation choices.
Clean and scale the data — treat missing values, duplicates, outliers, irrelevant variables, and inconsistent units before fitting the model.
Compare multiple algorithms — do not assume one method reveals the only valid structure; compare methods with different assumptions.
Tune parameters systematically — use suitable ranges, internal metrics, stability, and domain usefulness rather than arbitrary values.
Use more than one validation method — combine internal scores, visualisation, cluster profiles, repeated samples, external information, and expert judgement.
Check stability — repeat the analysis with different seeds, samples, and preprocessing choices; stable structures should appear consistently.
Interpret carefully — describe what the model found without claiming causation, and name clusters only after examining their features.
Audit ethical impact — check whether discovered groups create unfair treatment, hidden proxies, or harmful decisions.

content.text: K-means needs the number of clusters before training, and there is no single automatic answer. Analysts combine quantitative evidence with business usefulness.

The elbow method plots inertia — the total squared distance of observations from their assigned centroids. Inertia always falls as K rises, so a useful K often appears where the improvement begins to slow, forming an “elbow.”

content.caption: Figure 4. Elbow plot for K = 2 to 8. The bend at K = 4 gives a practical balance between compactness and simplicity.

content.text: The silhouette score compares how close a customer is to its own cluster versus other clusters. It approaches 1 when clusters are compact and well separated, approaches 0 when they overlap, and can turn negative when observations are poorly assigned.

content.caption: Figure 5. Silhouette scores across K = 2 to 8 — K = 4 gives the highest score, supporting the elbow result.

# Select customer features
X = df[['income', 'spending_score', 'frequency', 'recency', 'basket_value']]

# Scale the variables
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# Train the clustering model
model = KMeans(n_clusters=4, random_state=42, n_init=20)
df['cluster'] = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)

# Profile the results
profile = df.groupby('cluster')[X.columns].mean()
content.explanation: Scale first, fit K-means with a fixed random_state and several initialisations, then average each feature per cluster to build the profile.

content.text: Use a fixed random_state and multiple initialisations (n_init) so the result is less dependent on random starting centroids.

content.title: Read with care

content.text: Principal Component Analysis compresses the five scaled features into two components for visualisation. It shows cluster separation clearly but does not replace the original business interpretation.

content.caption: Figure 7. PCA projection of the five-dimensional customer space — the two components capture about 87% of the variance and show four well-separated groups.

content.text: Profiling turns anonymous cluster numbers into recognisable customer types. Comparing the average (centroid) feature levels across segments reveals each one's behavioural signature.

content.caption: Figure 8. Relative feature levels per segment — Premium Loyalists lead on income, spending, frequency, and basket, while At-Risk Customers stand out only on recency (long time since purchase).

content.text: Never name a cluster from only one feature. Use the full centroid/profile, the distribution of customers, and the business context.
content.title: Interpretation rule

content.text: A segment is only valuable when it leads to a distinct, feasible action. Each of the four discovered groups maps to its own business goal and playbook.

content.caption: Figure 9. Each segment maps to a clear business goal — Reward, Develop, Retain, or Recover — and a matching set of actions.

keyPoints: Customer segmentation groups similar customers without pre-existing labels, so it is an unsupervised-learning task that ends with human interpretation.
Good features describe value and behaviour — income, spending, frequency, recency, basket value — and identifiers like customer ID must be removed.
Because K-means uses distance, features must be standardised so large-range variables do not dominate.
Choose K with converging evidence: the elbow method, the silhouette score, cluster stability and size, and business interpretability (here, K = 4).
Profile each cluster with its full centroid, name it, and map it to a distinct business goal — Reward, Develop, Retain, or Recover.
Segments are data-dependent patterns, not permanent truths: monitor, refresh, and use them responsibly with attention to privacy and fairness.
commonMistakes: Clustering raw variables without scaling, letting income overwhelm frequency and recency.
Including customer ID or a transaction number as a numeric feature.
Naming a segment from a single feature instead of the full profile.
Trusting a high silhouette score as proof the segments are business-useful, or treating clusters as permanent, causal facts.
